name: VR headset
title: VR headset (standalone)
intro: This is a standalone VR headset. Explode it (🧩) to see the displays, lenses, tracking cameras, processor and cooling fan. Ask me "How does it know where I am?"
suggest: How does it know where I am?
looksLike: VR headset, VR goggles, virtual reality headset, MR headset

front_cover.name: Front cover
front_cover.info: The outermost cover panel, hiding the tracking cameras and cooling vents behind it.

housing.name: Housing
housing.info: The main body shell that encloses the internal parts and balances the headset's weight.

midframe.name: Midframe
midframe.info: The internal structural frame that holds the mainboard, lens modules and battery in precise alignment.

mainboard.name: Mainboard
mainboard.info: The main circuit board carrying the processor, memory, storage and wireless chips.

soc.name: Processor (SoC)
soc.info: A single chip combining CPU, GPU and AI processing. It renders two eye views over 90 times a second while tracking your head.

memory.name: Memory
memory.info: High-speed RAM holding data the processor is actively using; cleared when powered off.

storage.name: Storage
storage.info: Flash storage that keeps your apps, games and videos even when the power is off.

wifi.name: Wireless chip
wifi.info: Handles Wi-Fi networking and wireless controller connections without any cables.

heatsink.name: Heatsink
heatsink.info: A metal plate pressed against the processor to draw heat away so the fan can blow it out.

fan.name: Fan
fan.info: Draws hot air off the heatsink and vents it out of the headset.

fan_rotor.name: Fan blades
fan_rotor.info: High-speed fan blades that spin faster the harder the processor works.

cameras.name: Tracking cameras
cameras.info: Front cameras that constantly watch room features to calculate where your head is and track your hands.

depth_sensor.name: Depth sensor
depth_sensor.info: Measures the distance to real furniture and walls so virtual objects can rest on tables or hide behind walls.

battery.name: Battery
battery.info: Built-in rechargeable lithium battery providing about two hours of play.

flex_cables.name: Flex cables
flex_cables.info: Thin, flexible ribbon cables linking the displays, cameras and buttons to the mainboard.

ipd_rail.name: IPD rail
ipd_rail.info: Guide rail that lets the two lens modules slide sideways to match the distance between your eyes.

eye_carriage_l.name: Left lens module
eye_carriage_l.info: Combined left display and lens assembly that slides along the IPD rail.

eye_carriage_r.name: Right lens module
eye_carriage_r.info: Combined right display and lens assembly that slides along the IPD rail.

lens_l.name: Left lens
lens_l.info: Optical lens. Because the screen sits just centimetres from your eye, the lens refracts the light so the image appears over a metre away.

lens_r.name: Right lens
lens_r.info: Refracts light just like the left lens so your right eye can focus comfortably on the close-up screen.

display_l.name: Left display
display_l.info: Left-eye display panel. It shows a slightly different viewing angle than the right eye, which your brain fuses into 3D.

display_r.name: Right display
display_r.info: Right-eye display panel, working with the left display to create stereoscopic depth.

ipd_wheel.name: IPD wheel
ipd_wheel.info: Turning this wheel slides both lens modules inward or outward together to align with your pupils.

face_cushion.name: Face cushion
face_cushion.info: Soft facial interface pad that blocks outside light and cushions the headset against your face.

side_arms.name: Side arms
side_arms.info: Side arms extending back to hold the head strap and house the built-in speakers.

speakers.name: Speakers
speakers.info: Open-ear speakers built into the side arms that deliver directional spatial audio as you turn your head.

buttons.name: Buttons
buttons.info: External power and volume control buttons.

strap.name: Head strap
strap.info: Adjustable strap that spreads the headset's weight across your head so it doesn't press down on your nose.

steps.say: Each eye looks at its own display showing a slightly different angle, matching how your two eyes see the real world.

quiz.q: Why must the left and right eyes be shown slightly different images?
options: Your brain uses the difference between the two views to judge depth
This is binocular disparity: the closer an object is, the more the two eye views differ.
To make the image twice as bright
Brightness depends on the display panels; different angles create depth perception.
To save battery power
Rendering two separate views actually takes more computing power, all for depth perception.

steps.say: The screen sits just centimetres away, so optical lenses refract the light to place the virtual image over a metre out where your eyes can focus.

quiz.q: What happens if you remove the lenses and look straight at the screens a few centimetres away?
options: It's far too close for your eyes to focus, leaving everything blurry
Human eyes cannot focus closer than about 10 cm; the lenses optically move the image to a comfortable distance.
The image becomes larger and sharper
The lenses are what magnify and focus the image; without them it blurs out.
There is no difference at all
Without lenses refracting the light, your eyes cannot focus at such a short distance.

steps.say: Everyone's interpupillary distance (IPD) differs. Turning the IPD wheel slides both lens modules along the rail to centre them on your eyes.

track.title: How it knows where you are

steps.say: Front tracking cameras continuously scan the room, locking onto visual features like table corners and edges.

quiz.q: Without external room sensors, how does the headset know you just took a step forward?
options: Its cameras see the room's visual features shift backward
By tracking how surrounding landmarks move across the camera view, it calculates its own motion (inside-out tracking).
By satellite GPS
GPS signals can't penetrate indoors and have several metres of error.
By measuring Wi-Fi signal strength
Wi-Fi is for data networking and lacks the millimetre precision needed for head tracking.

steps.say: Hundreds of times a second, the processor fuses camera images with motion sensor data to calculate your pose and render the matching view.
The depth sensor maps the shape of the room so virtual objects can interact realistically with real floors and tables.
Running spatial tracking and dual high-frame-rate displays consumes heavy power, turning electrical energy into heat.
The metal heatsink conducts heat away from the processor, and the spinning fan blows that hot air out of the headset.

quiz.q: If cooling fails and the processor overheats, what happens first?
options: The processor throttles its speed down, causing the image to stutter
Thermal throttling slows the chip down to prevent damage, dropping the frame rate and causing motion sickness.
The battery explodes immediately
Built-in thermal protection throttles the chip first and shuts the power off before dangerous temperatures are reached.
The displays turn black and white
Overheating reduces frame rate and smoothness, not screen colour.

fan_dead.title: Cooling fan stopped
fan_dead.short: Gets hot and stutters after a few minutes
fan_dead.symptom: Ten minutes into a game, the headset gets very hot and the image starts stuttering badly. Look inside: what's broken?
fan_dead.hint: Once heat reaches the heatsink, what blows that hot air out of the shell? Check the blades inside the round cooler.
fan_dead.observe: Overheating means heat is trapped inside. Look at the heatsink on top of the mainboard: what part on top of it isn't moving?
whys: A dead battery would shut the headset off completely. Since it runs for ten minutes before overheating, check the cooling assembly on the mainboard.
Look at the lens modules—the screens display fine at first, and only stutter once the processor overheats. Check the fan mounted on the heatsink.
fan_dead.cause: The cooling fan blades stopped spinning, leaving heat from the processor trapped in the heatsink with no airflow to vent it.
fan_dead.why: Why does a stopped cooling fan not only make the headset hot, but also make the visuals stutter?
fan_dead.answer: The chip heats up while drawing and relies on the heatsink and fan to vent it. When the fan stops, trapped heat forces the chip to slow down to protect itself, making the picture stutter.
reasons: The fan generates electricity for the screens, so stopping it starves them of power.
Airflow from the fan pushes the lenses into focus, so without wind the image shakes.
